newsitem.title: USA: Circuit City's CarMax IPO starts with gains.
newsitem.headline: Circuit City's CarMax IPO starts with gains.

text.p: Wall Street investors snapped up CarMax Group shares on their first day of trading Tuesday, driving up the market value of the Circuit City Stores Inc. unit that sells used cars and trucks in superstores.

CarMax, which was priced at $20 Monday night, rose as high as $22 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the most active stock with 11.5 million shares changing hands by late afternoon. It was up $1.125 at $21.125 in afternoon trading.

Cantor Fitzgerald IPO analyst Vince Slavin said the very large size of the offering -- which was raised to 21.86 milion from 18.86 million shares -- could hold down opening premiums and disguise strong demand from institutional investors.
Lead underwriter Morgan Stanley & Co. raised the estimated price range for the deal on Monday to $18 to $20 from $15 to $17 amid strong demand and finally priced the deal at $20.
Circuit City still owns about 80 percent of CarMax, which will remain a division of the consumer electronics retailer.

CarMax is aiming for the highly fragmented and lucrative used car industry. It currently operates six stores in the Southeast and a vehicle reconditioning centre in Orlando, Fla., which offer between 400 to 1,200 vehicles each. Prices are generally $500 to $1,000 below book value, defined by the National Automobile Dealers Association.
With the $400 million it will pocket from the IPO, CarMax plans to launch an ambitious expansion. It plans to have 80 to 90 superstores by the end of fiscal 2002, it said in its prospectus.
But despite high sales -- up 258 percent in fiscal 1996 to $275.9 million -- CarMax has yet to turn a profit. It also sees a loss for fiscal 1997, in part due to expansion plans.

Another positive sign for the company is the willingness by big automakers, including Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp., to deal with auto superstores, Natwest Markets retail analyst John McKenna said in a research report. That gives CarMax better access to vehicles and could give auto superstores access to new car sales, he said.

McKenna also said the $600 billion automotive retailing industry is a big enough sector to support competition. Wayne Huizenga, the Florida billionaire who proved he can consolidate and revolutionise an industry with Blockbuster Entertainment, also has set his sights on the used-car industry. His Republic Industries Inc. owns AutoNation USA.

"We estimate that if the auto superstores can capture just 10 percent market share of the new and used auto market, the top 50 markets can support at least 350 to 400 auto-superstores," McKenna's report said.
